data.caption: lisawellbeing.com
data.copy:
We are a tiny company in Guelph making beetroot capsules with one ingredient. The brands with the big budgets use five or six. Only one of those ingredients is beetroot. The rest are fillers.

My name is Thomas, and I'm the founder of BeetaMed Organic Beetroot.

My Aunt Margaret was the kind of person who had an opinion about everything — and was usually right about most of it.

She lived just outside the Niagara region her whole life. Had an allotment she'd tended since her 40s. And beetroot was always the thing she was most proud of. Rows of it, every year. She ate it most days, pressed jars of it into everyone's hands at Christmas, and never stopped telling me I should be eating more of it.

I smiled. Said thanks. And largely ignored her.

But something stuck with me. Aunt Margaret was in her mid-70s and still walking three miles every morning. Still sharp. Still full of energy while plenty of people around her were slowing down and struggling.

Eventually I started wondering. Was it actually the beetroot?

So I looked into it. And what I found was genuinely surprising.

Beetroot is one of the richest natural sources of dietary nitrates. Your body converts those nitrates into nitric oxide — the molecule that keeps your blood vessels open and your circulation working properly. After 60, your body can make less and less nitric oxide on its own. That's a big part of why energy drops and joints stiffen up as you get older.

Beetroot also contains compounds called betalains — natural anti-inflammatories that may help with joint stiffness and everyday aching.

Aunt Margaret didn't know the science. She just knew it worked.

Turns out she was right all along.

So I started eating beetroot every day myself. Lasted about a week. The mess. Purple fingers. Purple chopping board. Kitchen towels completely ruined. And doing it every single day just wasn't realistic.

Then I tried buying organic beetroot from the shops. Couldn't find it anywhere reliably. And that matter…

data.caption: How to stop your dog from peeing in the house?
data.copy:
I wasn't planning on sharing this publicly.
But I realized that what I went through might help others — especially fellow dog owners dealing with similar issues.

Bella has been a part of our family for years. She's sweet, loving, and incredibly smart.

But her peeing problem pushed us to a breaking point.

It started gradually.
A puddle by the door. Then marking the couch legs. Eventually, every corner became her bathroom.

I assumed it was just a phase…

I tried every solution I could find.

Belly bands that she wiggled out of. 
Enzyme cleaners by the gallon.
Pee pads she'd miss on purpose.
Professional trainers who cost a fortune.

Nothing made a lasting difference…

Then came the day everything escalated.

I'd been out for just 2 hours. Came home to find she'd peed on my landlord's brand new carpet installation.

The smell hit me at the door.
Not just one spot — multiple puddles, like she'd marked her entire territory while I was gone.

I was frantically scrubbing when I heard footsteps upstairs.
My landlord — doing his monthly inspection.
He walked in and his face said everything.

"This is the third carpet this year. The smell is seeping into other units."

What he said next left me speechless:
"You have 14 days to fix this… or rehome the dog. Otherwise, I'm keeping your deposit and you're out."

I sat in silence.
I love Bella. She's family.
But I'd already lost two deposits — and the idea of giving her up felt impossible.

I began researching everything I hadn't tried.

Anxiety meds.
Crate training bootcamps.
Even looked into a canine behaviorist — but $150/hour was out of reach.
I was out of time.

In desperation, I brought Bella to a local rescue center.
I was heartbroken.

I explained the situation to a staff member named Sarah.

She listened carefully… then said something unexpected:

"I think there's still a way to fix this."

Bella was already stress-marking in the lobby.

data.caption: ★☆☆☆☆ pour la copie. Puis j'ai trouvé l'original.
data.copy:
★☆☆☆☆ « Aucun effet. Aucune différence sur mes douleurs de dos. Rien. La chaleur est à peine perceptible, la vibration s'arrête dès qu'on met le poids du corps dessus, et le dos est aussi raide après qu'avant. Argent jeté par la fenêtre. »
 
Cet avis, c'est moi qui l'ai écrit sur Trustpilot.
 
Pour un appareil à 69 euros qui ressemblait presque exactement à celui que je tiens sur la photo. Même forme. Mêmes promesses. Mais pas le même appareil.
 
Si tu as des problèmes de dos et que tu as abandonné après avoir été déçu par un appareil bon marché — tu as peut-être fait la même erreur que moi.
 
J'ai des problèmes de dos depuis des années. Cette pression sourde et constante dans le bas du dos. Ce tiraillement qui descend dans la jambe. La raideur du matin qu'on finit par accepter comme normale, parce qu'on croit que ça fait partie de l'âge.
 
Mon médecin traitant a appelé ça de « l'usure. » Il m'a prescrit du Doliprane et envoyée chez le kiné. Six séances remboursées en partie par la Sécu. Ensuite il faut une nouvelle ordonnance et reprendre rendez-vous — des semaines d'attente. Le parcours classique.
 
La kiné a aidé un peu. Pendant deux jours. Puis tout est revenu.
 
Il y a quelques mois, ma voisine Monique a mentionné en passant qu'elle avait trouvé quelque chose pour son dos. Quelque chose qu'elle utilisait chaque soir.
 
J'ai remarqué qu'elle se déplaçait autrement. Plus droite. Plus cette démarche hésitante que je lui connaissais. Comme si quelque chose avait réellement changé.
 
Je n'ai rien demandé de plus. Mais l'idée ne m'a pas quittée.
 
Une semaine plus tard, j'ai tapé dans Google « appareil pour le dos avec chaleur et massage. » Des dizaines de résultats. Tous se ressemblaient. Tous promettaient la même chose. J'en ai choisi un à 69 euros avec de bonnes évaluations.
 
Il a fallu presque quatre semaines pour le recevoir.
 
Quatre semaines à attendre, pendant que le dos empirait jour…

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
